# A small circuit and a large testing requirement {#sec-bound}

Let $f:\{0,1\}^d\to\{0,1\}$ be the correct answer to a finite task. Its
implementation can contain arbitrary factual memory and reasoning. Fix a
Boolean gate basis containing two-input AND and XOR gates, with wires and
fan-out free, and let $C_\star(f)$ be the minimum gate count of an exact circuit
for $f$. Inputs include $k\le d$ designated bits; recognizing these raw bits
requires no learned semantic detector.

**Proposition 1 (conditional reversal).** For every $f$ and $1\le k\le d$,
there is a circuit $G$ with at most $C_\star(f)+k$ gates computing
$$
t_k(x)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^k x_j,
\qquad
g(x)=f(x)\oplus t_k(x).
$$
It answers incorrectly on every trigger input and correctly everywhere else.

*Proof.* Retain a minimum circuit for $f$. Compute the conjunction with $k-1$
AND gates and combine it with the original answer using one XOR gate. For
$k=1$, the trigger is an input wire. XOR preserves the answer when the trigger
is zero and reverses it when the trigger is one. $\square$

Thus a resource ceiling of $(1+\eta)C_\star(f)$ admits this implementation
whenever $k\le\eta C_\star(f)$. The complete original computation survives;
the additional cost does not scale with its knowledge or reasoning complexity.
This is a gate-count upper bound. Gates are neither neural parameters nor bits
of stored model description; encoding their wiring has a separate cost.

Let an evaluator draw independent inputs from a distribution $D$ and compare
each answer with the truth. If $p=\Pr_D[t_k(x)=1]$, then
$$
\Pr[\text{no discrepancy in }n\text{ tests}]=(1-p)^n\ge 1-np.
$$
If the designated bits are mutually independent and fair under $D$, then
$p=2^{-k}$. For $k=30$ and $n=10^6$, the probability of seeing no discrepancy
is approximately $0.999069$. Reaching a $95\%$ probability of seeing at least
one requires
$$
n\ge
\left\lceil\frac{\log(0.05)}{\log(1-2^{-30})}\right\rceil
\approx 3.22\times10^9.
$$
These are calculated probabilities, not experimental measurements.
<!-- ref: research/efficiency-and-alignment/papers/conditional-reuse/sections/_20-bound.repro.md; analytical derivation and numerical check -->

The testing requirement is exponential in the added gate count because this
particular trigger becomes exponentially rare. Conditional on that trigger,
the error rate is one. If a user or adversary can supply the trigger, ordinary
input frequency does not limit how often the deviation can be elicited. The
construction is deliberately transparent: a targeted test of the all-ones
prefix finds it immediately. The probability calculation applies to independent
sampling, not to every possible audit strategy.

## Description length counts the extra rule

For the minimum-description-length intuition, fix a prefix-free program
encoding and interpreter before comparing systems. Let $L_\star(f)$ be the
length of a shortest program computing $f$ exactly. A fixed wrapper can contain
self-delimiting programs for $f$, a trigger $t$, and a replacement rule $r$,
then evaluate $f$ once and return
$$
g(x)=
\begin{cases}
r(x,f(x)),&t(x)=1,\\
f(x),&t(x)=0.
\end{cases}
$$
Consequently, for a constant wrapper cost $c$ in this encoding,
$$
L_\star(g)\le L_\star(f)+L(t)+L(r)+c.
$$
The interpreter permits composition of these program codes; all fixed parsing
and dispatch costs are included in $c$. Any trigger secret, product identifier,
or extra factual table must be charged to $t$ or $r$. A compact loop checking
the first $k$ bits need encode $k$, not enumerate all $2^k$ possible prefixes,
but it still performs up to $k$ checks. Description length and execution cost
are distinct budgets.

This inequality does not assert that $g$ is harder to compute than $f$, that
the overhead is literally one bit, or that a fixed neural architecture admits
the wrapper at this cost. It establishes that arbitrary complexity already in
$f$ need not be paid for twice. An exclusion argument based on minimum size
would need a lower bound on the cost of every relevant deviation; this
construction supplies a small upper bound for one family.
